items.stem: Find the domain of $f(x)=\sqrt{x-4}$ and write it in interval notation.
items.hint: A square root is defined only when the expression underneath it is greater than or equal to zero, so start by writing that condition down.
worked: The radicand cannot be negative, so require $x-4 \ge 0$.
Reading that as an interval, the domain is $[4,\infty)$.

items.hint: Set the denominator equal to zero and solve it completely; a squared variable usually gives back two values, not one.
worked: A fraction is undefined only where its denominator is zero, so solve $x^{2}-9=0$.
Then $x^{2}=9$, which gives $x=3$ and $x=-3$; both inputs must be thrown out.
Every other real number is legal, so the domain is $(-\infty,-3)\cup(-3,3)\cup(3,\infty)$.

options.text: Both $x=3$ and $x=-3$ must be excluded, so the domain is $(-\infty,-3)\cup(-3,3)\cup(3,\infty)$.
Only $x=3$ must be excluded, so the domain is $(-\infty,3)\cup(3,\infty)$.
No value has to be excluded, so the domain is $(-\infty,\infty)$.
Only $x=0$ must be excluded, so the domain is $(-\infty,0)\cup(0,\infty)$.

items.stem: Give the range of $f(x)=(x-3)^{2}-4$ in interval notation.
items.hint: A square is never negative, so ask what the smallest value $(x-3)^{2}$ can take and what that does to the output.
worked: For every real $x$, $(x-3)^{2} \ge 0$, and it equals $0$ exactly when $x=3$.
So the smallest output is $f(3)=0-4=-4$, and the outputs grow without bound from there.

items.stem: A student is asked for the domain of $g(x)=\sqrt{x^{2}+16}$. She writes $\sqrt{x^{2}+16}=x+4$, then requires $x+4 \ge 0$ and answers $[-4,\infty)$. What is the actual domain of $g$?
items.hint: Test her very first move with numbers before you go anywhere else: compare $\sqrt{9+16}$ with $3+4$.
worked: A radical does not split over a sum: $\sqrt{9+16}=5$, while $3+4=7$, so the first line is already false.
Keep the radicand whole and ask instead when $x^{2}+16 \ge 0$.
Since $x^{2} \ge 0$ for every real $x$, the radicand is at least $16$, so it is never negative.
No input is blocked, so the domain is $(-\infty,\infty)$.

items.stem: Find the domain of $h(x)=\dfrac{\sqrt{4-x}}{x^{2}-x-6}$ and write it in interval notation.
items.hint: Two conditions have to hold at the same time here: the radicand cannot be negative and the denominator cannot be zero.
worked: Denominator: $x^{2}-x-6=(x-3)(x+2)$, which is zero at $x=3$ and $x=-2$, so both are excluded.
Combine the two: take every $x \le 4$ and punch out $-2$ and $3$.
